claims: "Pied-à-terre" is French for "foot on the ground".
A pied-à-terre is a secondary residence that is not the owner's primary address.
As of April 2026, New York State officials are negotiating a "pied-à-terre tax" as part of the state budget.
New York State has a projected $5.4 billion budget deficit.
Governor Hochul and city officials are proposing a yearly surcharge on residential properties worth $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence.
The pied-à-terre tax primarily targets non-residents, international buyers, or wealthy individuals who use luxury condos as occasional homes.
The pied-à-terre tax is intended to generate roughly $500 million annually.
The term "pied-à-terre" originated in the 18th century.
The term "pied-à-terre" referred to soldiers who would dismount their horses ("mettre pied à terre") to occupy temporary lodging.
